# Open and closed sets in Euclidean space

Open balls define interior points, open sets, closed sets, boundaries, and closures in Euclidean space.

## Exercises

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-any-ball-open}

Show that any $\epsilon$-ball is open.

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-closed}

Show that $A \cup \partial A$ is closed.

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-if-closed-then-if-sequence-converges}

Show that if $A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is closed and a sequence $\mathbf{x}_i \in A$ converges to some $\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n$, then $\mathbf{x}\in A$. This gives an equivalent characterization of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-closure-smallest-closed-set-contains-equal}

Show that the closure of $A$, the smallest closed set $\bar{A}$ that contains $A$, is equal to $A\cup \partial A$.

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-closed-2}

Show that $$A = \{ (x,0) \mid x \in [-1,1] \} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$$ is closed.

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-neither-open-nor-closed-boundary-interior}

Show that $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is neither open nor closed. Show that the boundary of $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{R}$. Show that the interior of $\mathbb{Q}$ is empty. What is the closure of $\mathbb{Q}$?

:::

:::{#exr-open-and-closed-sets-compute-interior-boundary-closure}

Let $$A = \{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid 0 \leq x < 1, \quad 0 \leq y < 1\}.$$ Compute the interior of $A$, the boundary of $A$, the closure of $A$.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="tutor"}

## Solutions

### Tutor note: Open and closed sets in Euclidean space

**Tutor note:** This exercise really develops the basic skills thinking about open and closed sets, and also mathematical argumentation. Even if the exercises are fairly basic by undergrad maths standards, maybe this style of thinking is difficult for some students, and therefore I think it is worthwhile.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-any-ball-open

Let $A = B_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_0)$ and $\mathbf{x}\in A$. Set $r = \|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0\| < \epsilon$ and $\delta = \epsilon-r>0$. If $\mathbf{y}\in B_\delta(\mathbf{x})$, then

$$
\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}_0\|
\leq \|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_0\|
<\delta+r=\epsilon.
$$

Thus $B_\delta(\mathbf{x})\subset A$. Every point of $A$ has an open ball contained in $A$, so $A$ is open.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-closed

Let $C=(A\cup\partial A)^\complement$. If $\mathbf{x}\in C$, then $\mathbf{x}\notin A$ and $\mathbf{x}\notin\partial A$. Since $\mathbf{x}$ is not a boundary point, some ball $B_\epsilon(\mathbf{x})$ lies wholly in $A$ or wholly in $A^\complement$. It cannot lie in $A$ because it contains $\mathbf{x}$, so it lies in $A^\complement$ and contains no boundary point. Hence $B_\epsilon(\mathbf{x})\subset C$. The complement $C$ is open, so $A\cup\partial A$ is closed.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-closure-smallest-closed-set-contains-equal

We have shown that $A \cup \partial A$ is closed. Suppose $A \cup \partial A$ is not the smallest closed set that contains $A$, i.e., $(A\cup\partial A)\setminus\bar{A}$ contains some point $\mathbf{x}$. Since both sets contain $A$, we must have $\mathbf{x}\in \partial A$. From this, we should look for a contradiction, because intuitively, the boundary must be part of $\bar{A}$. For all $\epsilon>0$, $B_\epsilon(\mathbf{x})$ intersects both $A$ and $A^\complement$. Therefore, there exists a sequence $\mathbf{x}_i\in A$ such that $\mathbf{x}_i \to \mathbf{x}\in  \partial A$, but the smallest closed set containing $A$ must contain this $\mathbf{x}$.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-closed-2

Consider $A^\complement$, the plane without the interval $[-1,1]$ on the $x$-axis. For a point $(x,y)\in A^\complement$ with $y\neq0$, choose any $0<\epsilon<|y|$. If $y=0$, then $|x|>1$, and we may choose any $0<\epsilon<|x|-1$. In either case, the $\epsilon$-ball around $(x,y)$ misses $A$. Thus $A^\complement$ is open and $A$ is closed.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-neither-open-nor-closed-boundary-interior

Let $p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$ be a rational number, and let $]p/q-\epsilon, p/q + \epsilon[$ be an $\epsilon$-"ball" around $p/q$. But we know that between any two real numbers, there are infinitely many rational numbers, and also irrational numbers. Hence, the ball is not contained in $\mathbb{Q}$, so the rational numbers do not form an open set. Hence no rational number has an open ball around it, and hence the interior of $\mathbb{Q}$ is empty. To show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not closed, consider the openness of the complement, $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, the irrational numbers. The same argument can be applied, the irrationals are not open.

The boundary of $\mathbb{Q}$ is all of $\mathbb{R}$, since any ball around a rational number contains both rational and irrational numbers.

Finally, the closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ is then $\mathbb{R}$.

### Solution to @exr-open-and-closed-sets-compute-interior-boundary-closure

The interior of $A$ is $$\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid 0 < x < 1, \quad 0 < y < 1\}.$$ The boundary of $A$ is the border of the square, $$\partial A = \{ (0,t) \mid 0 \leq t \leq 1 \} \cup \{ (1,t) \mid 0 \leq t \leq 1 \} \cup \{ (t,0) \mid 0 \leq t \leq 1 \} \cup \{ (t,1) \mid 0 \leq t \leq 1 \}$$ The closure of $A$ is $A$ with the border, hence $$\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1\}.$$

:::
